stances.claim: Commissioner Dulay correctly distinguished nonstock-nonprofit schools from other corporations/associations granted tax exemption by ordinary statute (the NIRC) -- because the Constitution itself grants NNS the tax exemption directly, with only two simple requirements (nonstock-nonprofit organization + revenues used actually/directly/exclusively for educational purposes), and the BIR cannot add or vary these constitutional requirements.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-vs-statutory-source distinction (BIR cannot add to constitutional grants)

stances.claim: While critics complain that RMO 44-2016's documentary requirements are too bureaucratic, they are 'few and reasonable' compared to the earlier RMO 20-2013, requiring only: (1) SEC + CHED/DepEd/TESDA certification of current operation in good standing, and (2) proof that funds are spent for educational purposes only -- both necessary for satisfying the two constitutional requisites.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-baseline defense (the new RMO is improvement over the old, not perfection)

stances.claim: Private nonstock-nonprofit schools fill the constitutional education gap that the state cannot fill alone -- the state allocates the largest budget portion to education and education is compulsory for all children of school age, but the budget is still insufficient; NNS therefore deserve not only tax exemption but financial assistance, especially those catering to basic education.
stances.rhetorical_move: gap-filling-as-constitutional-cooperation argument (state's duty + NNS contribution → not just exemption but assistance)

stances.claim: The CEAP (founded 1941, 1,252 members, ~700 mission schools for the poor) and ACSCU (organized 1946, 118 members) embody the institutional reach of religious-school nonprofit education in PH -- and any Muslim equivalent appears absent locally, leaving a gap in inter-religious institutional infrastructure.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-census framing with noted-absence (Muslim school association gap)

notable_anecdotes: The two simple constitutional requisites repeatedly emphasized -- 'actually, directly and exclusively used for educational purposes' becoming the column's leitmotif, repeated in different syntactic positions to anchor the test.

The BIR-cannot-add-to-Constitution principle: 'The Bureau of Internal Revenue cannot add, much less vary, the two simple requirements of the Constitution' -- the column's most concise statement of administrative-vs-constitutional hierarchy.
The state's allocation of biggest annual budget portion to education, yet budget insufficient -- using the budget reality to physicalize the gap-filling role of private NNS.

CEAP's 75-year-old status, 1,252 members with ~700 mission schools 'offering basic education to the poor and the marginalized' -- quantifying the Catholic-school sector's reach into underserved communities.
ACSCU's institutional breakdown -- 6 universities, 3 seminaries, 40 colleges, 69 basic education schools -- providing a textured snapshot of Protestant educational infrastructure.

The noted absence of a PH Muslim school association: 'Although there is an Association of Muslim Schools in the world, I am not aware of any Philippine affiliate' -- a careful epistemic disclosure rather than absolute claim.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban commends Internal Revenue Commissioner Caesar R. Dulay for issuing Revenue Memorandum Order 44-2016 on July 25, 2016, within his first month in office, clarifying that nonstock-nonprofit educational institutions (NNS) are constitutionally exempt from tax on all revenues used 'actually, directly and exclusively for educational purposes,' and excluding them from the strict conditions of the earlier RMO 20-2013 (July 22, 2013) that had lumped NNS with corporations and associations granted exemption only by the NIRC. Dulay correctly distinguished the two sources: NNS exemption flows directly from the Constitution, requiring only two simple requisites -- (1) nonstock-nonprofit organization, and (2) revenues used actually, directly, and exclusively for educational purposes -- and 'the Bureau of Internal Revenue cannot add, much less vary' these constitutional requirements. Critics complain that the new RMO's documentary requirements (SEC + CHED/DepEd/TESDA certification of operation in good standing; proof that funds are spent for educational purposes only) remain bureaucratic, but they are 'few and reasonable' compared to RMO 20-2013. The Constitution mandates the state to 'establish and maintain a system of free public education in the elementary and high school level,' with elementary compulsory; the state allocates the biggest budget portion to education yet still falls short, and private NNS fill the gap, relieving the state of its constitutional duty. CJ argues the state should not only exempt but financially assist these schools, especially those catering to basic education, since their tuition and donations 'really, directly and ultimately benefit the children, and indirectly, the state.' These NNS are operated by Catholic dioceses and religious orders (Jesuits, Dominicans) and by foundations like the Tan Yan Kee, Metrobank, and Angeles University Foundations. CJ catalogs the institutional reach: the 75-year-old Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines (CEAP, founded 1941) has 1,252 members of which about 700 are mission schools for the poor and marginalized; the Association of Christian Schools, Colleges and Universities (ACSCU, organized 1946) has 118 members (6 universities, 3 seminaries, 40 colleges, 69 basic-education schools); and while there is a global Association of Muslim Schools, CJ is not aware of any local PH affiliate. RMO 44-2016 benefits all religious schools that can document the two constitutional requisites.
